Jagnesh told the court that the man who has four children, has no counsel at that time he was charged in court and asked for a lower bail.
However, Deputy Public Prosecutor Fazriel Fardiansyah Abdul Kadir objected the application but if the court allow the application, Fazriel had suggested the bail sum of RM10,000.
Meanwhile, a 42-year-old man was fined RM100 or seven days’ jail for failing to explain how he had in possession the three packets of instant drinks believed to be stolen.

Azmi Mohd Ayub@ Md Ayub pleaded guilty before Magistrate Dzul Helmy Yunus, to failing to give reasonable explanation about the instant drinks at 11pm on November 12 this year at a supermarket in Lido, Penampang. — Daily Express
2294f6fd69318614: NOVEMBER 20 — Does anyone still care about Bersih? I have been wondering. Ten years ago, on November 19, 2016, Malaysians came out in yellow for Bersih 5.
Bersih, the electoral reform coalition that grew into something much larger, turns 20 this month.
I had hoped to feel a little happier about the anniversary, but looking at where Malaysian politics has taken us, I find myself with rather mixed feelings.
I have spent a rather large part of my academic life with Bersih: a doctoral thesis, an academic book, journal articles, public commentaries, and numerous media interviews over the years.
When I started, some wondered why I took a protest movement so seriously. Would it last? Could it really change anything? Was it worth spending years studying?
Those were also years when the political climate was far less forgiving, when even being associated with a protest movement could invite intimidation.
Maybe I was naive, but I believed there was something important happening among those ordinary Malaysians who had decided to come together.

We have a much longer history of protest than we sometimes care to remember. There were the demonstrations against the Malayan Union in 1946, the Teluk Gong land struggle in 1967, the farmers’ protests and student demonstrations in Baling in 1974, Reformasi in 1998, Hindraf in 2007, the anti-Lynas movement and Himpunan Hijau in the early 2010s, alongside countless labour, environmental and student struggles.
These movements had different grievances, political orientations and visions of the country.

Bersih belonged to this larger history, but did something remarkable in its own right. It brought Malaysians who disagreed about plenty of other things together around a common demand: clean and fair elections.
Of course there were interests involved. Parties saw opportunities, organisers disagreed, and participants carried different hopes into the crowd.
Movements are coalitions, not collections of saints. I have written about those tensions myself. But treating Bersih as merely opposition politics misses what happened among ordinary people.

I think of the yellow gatherings organised by Malaysians overseas, far from Kuala Lumpur. And in May 2018, when postal ballots arrived so late that volunteers carried them on flights, passed them from person to person, and delivered them to returning officers. People changed their plans to carry somebody else’s vote. They simply believed the ballot mattered.
I still find that more moving than most speeches about patriotism.
One thing I have learned from studying social movements is that their significance cannot be measured simply by whether they succeed in changing a government or achieving their demands.
Sometimes their more enduring contribution lies in how people begin to see themselves, their place in politics, and what they can accomplish together.
I think those small acts of solidarity, including the extraordinary effort to bring postal ballots home, tell us something about that.

Not everyone involved was necessarily a Bersih activist, and that is precisely the beauty of a movement. It would be a terrible mistake to judge all of that simply by what became of the politicians who later came to power.
Then came 2018. A government changed, and we had reason to hope something deeper might change too.

Yet the years since have shown us how flexible Malaysian politics can be when powerful people need one another. Former enemies become coalition partners. Old declarations are quietly revised. We are told this is maturity, the necessary art of compromise.
What I find particularly disheartening is the possibility that we have not only lost our appetite for street protests, but also our faith in what they can achieve.
I have heard the argument that Malaysians are doing reasonably well economically, so there is little reason to take to the streets anymore. I wish it were that simple.

It is rather convenient to mistake the absence of protests for public satisfaction. People may still be angry, disappointed, or deeply concerned about the direction of the country, but no longer believe that gathering in the streets will make much difference.
Also, it hardly helps that we continue to associate protests with chaos and violence, as though citizens gathering peacefully are somehow a danger to society.

Violence should never be excused, but peaceful assembly is a constitutional right under Article 10. What troubles me is not simply that fewer people seem willing to protest, but that we may be losing faith in one of the very ways ordinary Malaysians once believed they could change their country.
Anwar Ibrahim’s political life is inseparable from Reformasi, yet his government now includes Barisan Nasional (BN).

In April, three activists were arrested after protesting during the anti-corruption chief’s speech. In August, groups gathered outside the Home Ministry to demand progress on reforming the Peaceful Assembly Act. We are still protesting the restrictions on protest.

And now Najib Razak is home, though still under house arrest. But on the tenth anniversary of Bersih 5, it is hard not to think of the thousands who took to the streets demanding accountability, and to wonder what they are thinking now. What a strange anniversary this has become.
None of this means Bersih achieved nothing. Undi18 and automatic voter registration widened participation.

In 2025, the Federal Court struck down the criminal penalty for failing to notify the police ahead of an assembly. These are real gains. Bersih helped create a public that expected more. Disappointment should not make us careless about that history.

When I began studying Bersih, perhaps naively, I imagined that one day my research would feel like history. Instead, here I am, still asking many of the same questions, and wishing we had moved further than we have.
Could there be another Bersih? I don’t know, and maybe we should not expect the next generation to recreate what came before.

Movements emerge from their own circumstances, and younger Malaysians will have their own grievances and ways of making themselves heard. Some may even find themselves protesting against people who once marched in yellow.

* Khoo Ying Hooi, PhD, is an Associate Professor at Universiti Malaya. Her doctoral research on the Bersih movement was published as a book in 2020, titled, “The Bersih Movement and Democratisation in Malaysia: Repression, Dissent and Opportunities”.
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
c1bc16b70ede5f6f: Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04.

Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. Yes, we know, we have heard this before: we reported on his plans last month. But this time, there's the beginning of a release schedule.

Seager said that Ubuntu Core is already out there in tens of thousands of IoT devices – which seems like a modest estimate to us, and to him too, as he quickly added "maybe more." Despite some noise a few years ago, though, what's still missing is the desktop version.
Seager's slides listed three bullet points: that Core Desktop will be "immutable," "composable," and "attestable."

As he put it, they are "taking the whole of the Linux operating system, and cramming the whole thing into snaps." Acknowledging that this is going to be wildly controversial, he said: "This is one for the Redditors."

He's right. There is a lot of resistance to snap, and in direct response, advocacy of the Red Hat-backed Flatpak instead – but we have seen almost none that is based on either system's technical merits. Much of that opposition concerns claims of one being more open than the other. We've looked at how both systems work, and our impression is that the implementation of snap is cleaner, simpler, easier to use, and more comprehensible. Snap does depend on systemd, which Flatpak does not – but only for now. Flatpak NG is in development and will also need everyone's favorite init system.
Ubuntu Core's immutability is not new technology: even Core 16 is now a decade old. It has supported in-place version upgrades since Core 22.

We have reported before that Canonical remains strongly committed to its packaging format, and that commitment seems stronger than ever. Seager continued: "Never has a model like snap confinement been more relevant… we're finally in a position where we can bring this to the desktop."

The core idea of an immutable OS is that "much more of the system is not writable at runtime," meaning that it "can't be messed with once the system has booted." He talked about the same three use cases we discussed last month. The "browser-centric machine" is the company's analog to Google ChromeOS, and he said that it's essentially ready now, suggesting that everyone listening probably has a family member whose computer is basically just a way to use a web browser.

The second was the dedicated games machine, which we interpret as a response to Valve's SteamOS. This edition, he said, would "boot straight to Steam," with "just enough of a shell to launch games." There's also an immutable "development workstation," and here, he offered the example of developers who need to work on some long-unsupported hardware or software, for whom an immutable OS means that you "can't brick your system by installing some weird old dependencies, unmaintained for 20 years."

Another important benefit is "atomic, transactional updates," which he said "brings enormous stability." The terminology comes from the database world: an atomic operation succeeds as a whole or is not applied. The aim is to avoid leaving the system stranded between incompatible package versions, with rollback providing a route back if an update causes trouble.
The "composable" part means assembling the OS from separately packaged components, from desktop environments to underlying services such as PipeWire and fingerprint-reader support.

Here, Seager used an example that spoke to us. He asked: "Ever installed something and watch as it spewed stuff all over your system?" Yes, we have, many, many times. You install one innocent-seeming little component, and it brings in a database, three new server components, and about half of a different desktop environment. We mentioned an example when we described how to customize Xfce a couple of months ago. That time around, in Debian, we found it was safe to install all packages starting with "xfce4-" except "xfce4-dev-tools." Most are tiny panel controls taking just hundreds of kilobytes, but the "dev-tools" package also pulls in several hundred megabytes of compilers, linkers, and other programming tools, totally unrelated to desktop layouts – and once installed, they're surprisingly tricky to remove again.

This is part of the appeal of a composable immutable OS: adding a component need not mean tangling its dependencies into the base system. But easier housekeeping isn't the only attraction. Canonical kept snap packages from its cancelled phone and tablet OS because snaps enable it to maintain a single package of, for instance, Firefox, which will work on all of its different OS versions that are still getting updates. Moving such important external dependencies into isolated snap packages makes it easier and safer to upgrade from one version of the OS to another. Complex sets of dependencies are the main point of failure of OS upgrades, especially when the OS has been used for a while.

This is very much not a solved problem. For instance, Debian version upgrades can be fraught – especially when the installation has decades of history behind it. Debian does at least support version-to-version upgrades. For many years and versions, RHEL did not – which is why we highlighted AlmaLinux's tooling for the task. Zorin OS added version-to-version upgrades in 16.3 just a few years ago. Linux Mint introduced its own upgrade tooling a few years earlier, although it still imposes restrictions.

It's a tough issue to crack. Major enterprise vendors discourage it, and phone OSes are all immutable. Helping with this problem is one of the main reasons snap packaging exists, while Flatpak is almost entirely irrelevant to it.

Seager also stated that Core Desktop would support "multiple desktops from the start." This will not be a GNOME-only project. Indeed, he specifically mentioned a KDE Plasma version, saying: "Plasma is great. People love it. We will have a KDE edition, with rolling Plasma. We will deliver upstream Plasma, as fast as we can." That sounds like a very welcome counterpoint to the LTS version of Plasma 6.6 in Kubuntu 26.04 whose announcement we covered back in August.

For the "attestable" line of the slide, he claimed that Core Desktop was "evolving the way we think about 'trust' on a machine. We have TPM, secure boot, TPM-backed Full Disk Encryption… but they're all bolt-ons." Core Desktop, he added, could "tie this into a hardware root of trust," delivering "verified system integrity." Canonical revived its TPM-backed full-disk encryption system back in 2025, and it arrived in Ubuntu 26.04. Back in January, systemd creator Lennart Poettering launched his startup Amutable, and earlier this month published a technical overview of its new immutable Linux. We suspect Canonical is watching closely, and that this is a hint in that direction.

We were also amused by Seager's mention of another rather niche distro: he said that Core Desktop would deliver "all of the joy that people derive from NixOS, for those with that perverse habit – but for everybody."

Daily preview installation images of Core Desktop will, apparently, be available very soon, in both GNOME and KDE flavors, and he warned that "there be dragons." (That may be a veiled nod to one of founder Mark Shuttleworth's other companies.)

After the promises made in 2023, we'll be watching that timetable closely. "I believe this is the future of Linux," Seager said, promising "a final version by 28.04, released alongside Ubuntu," adding that a "very stretchy stretch goal was by default for 30.04: download from ubuntu.com and you get Core Desktop – unless you ask for the other thing."
For those alarmed by that prospect, he had reassurance: "Ubuntu as you know it today is not going anywhere. There are no plans for the existing distro to go away."

Core Desktop wasn't even the main subject of his keynote. They followed a lengthy excursion into formal logic: definitions, proofs, invariants, and designing software whose behavior can be checked against precisely stated rules. The accompanying slides showed the logos of organizations working in this area, such as Hegel, Antithesis, and the Lean programming language. For now, an entire OS is much too big to formally verify, but subcomponents may be doable – and Canonical is starting with snapd.

He also expressed his satisfaction with the Stonking release, highlighting that it advanced Canonical's move toward Rust-based components, including Rustls and upki – noting that this proved very timely in the light of recent events. The release also delivered the newest available kernel, OpenSSL 4 – which he called a "huge change" – and official RISC-V images. He also called out the Myna speech-recognition feature, saying that it was all in-house, designed and shipped in six months by a team of "about two and a half people." It will form part of the company's plans for what it calls a context-aware desktop. ®
8c2dc0f6a66eda60: KOTA KINABALU, Nov 20 — The provision of a qibla (direction of prayer) marker on Mount Kinabalu is a basic facility for Muslims to perform prayers and is not intended to grant exclusive rights to any religion, said Sabah Mufti Datuk Dr Bungsu @ Aziz Jaafar.

In a statement today, he explained that the presence of the marker indicating the direction of Kaabah did not mean that the rights of followers of other religions to practise their respective faiths on the mountain were being denied or sidelined.
“The presence of the qibla marker does not in any way prevent followers of other religions from praying or practising their respective faiths on the mountain.

“There is no such thing as exclusive privileges for any particular religion on Mount Kinabalu,” he said, adding that anyone could engage in religious activities, subject to their needs and approval from Sabah Parks.

Bungsu said the installation of a qibla marker was also not carried out arbitrarily, as it required official verification from an authorised body such as the Department of Islamic Development Malaysia (Jakim) or the relevant religious department to ensure its directional accuracy.

He said followers of other religions, including Christians, Hindus, Buddhists and those of other faiths, are welcomed to submit proposals for specific facilities to Sabah Parks management for consideration, subject to suitability and park regulations.

On the issue of fairness to followers of all religions, he explained that equal treatment should not be measured by providing identical facilities for all religious practices. Instead, it should ensure that every visitor is respected and given the space to practise their faith without infringing on the rights of others.

“The public should not confuse the provision of facilities for one religion with granting privileges that deny the rights of other religions, as the qibla marker is merely a directional guide and facility, not an obligation,” he said.

However, he stressed that safety and compliance with the standard operating procedures (SOP) for climbing activities remained the absolute priority and must not be compromised by any religious or cultural activities.

He also reminded the public that Mount Kinabalu remained open to all segments of society, and that the responsibility of safeguarding the safety and sustainability of the natural treasure must be shared by everyone.
Previously, the installation of a qibla direction marker on Mount Kinabalu went viral on social media, becoming a topic of discussion among netizens. — Bernama
ecc19f90b11b8ba7: SEREMBAN, Nov 20 — Negeri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim has clarified that he never authorised the submission of his resignation letter to Yang Dipertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, contrary to reports on Monday.
He said the letter had been kept by the party leadership but stressed that he had never consented to its submission under such circumstances.
“I did not personally submit the resignation letter to His Royal Highness. The letter was indeed kept by the party leadership, but I never agreed to it being submitted in that manner.

“I only learnt about it through social media, and His Royal Highness also did not accept the way it was done. I neither submitted nor consented to the letter being presented to His Royal Highness. I do not even know who delivered it,” he told a press conference at the Menteri Besar’s official residence here today.

Earlier, Ismail was granted an audience with Tuanku Muhriz at Istana Hinggap, which was also attended by Undang Luak Rembau Datuk Sedia Raja Datuk Hassan Ab Hamid, Undang Luak Sungai Ujong Datuk Klana Petra Datuk Muhammad Faris Johari and Undang Luak Jelebu Datuk Mendika Menteri Akhirulzaman Datuk Azrin Khairi.
Following the audience, Ismail, who is also Juasseh assemblyman, said Tuanku Muhriz had decreed that he continue serving as Menteri Besar to ensure continuity in the state administration.

The controversy over Ismail’s position arose on Monday night when Barisan Nasional (BN) secretary-general Datuk Seri Dr Zambry Abd Kadir, in a statement posted on BN’s official Facebook page, announced that the Menteri Besar had resigned.
Zambry said BN chairman and Umno president Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi had received a copy of the resignation letter purportedly addressed and sent to Tuanku Muhriz.
On Tuesday, the Negeri Sembilan Palace clarified that a Menteri Besar’s resignation would only take effect with the consent of Tuanku Muhriz, in accordance with the State Constitution.

Meanwhile, Ismail said the state government’s immediate priority was to restore the smooth functioning of its administration, which had been disrupted by the absence of State Executive Council (Exco) members.
He said the situation had prevented many government decisions from being made as the Exco meetings could not be held.

“The state administration has been significantly disrupted because there are no Exco members. Therefore, I will seek Tuanku Muhriz’s consent to appoint new Exco members as approved by His Royal Highness,” he said.
Ismail stressed that the appointments were subject to Tuanku Muhriz’s consent, adding that a list of proposed Exco members had yet to be prepared but would be finalised as soon as possible.
He said discussions on the dates of the State Legislative Assembly sittings, including the tabling of the state budget, would only take place after the Exco appointments were settled.

On adat issues linked to the state’s political turmoil, Ismail said such issues should be resolved through the appropriate adat procedures without disrupting the administration of the state government. — Bernama
830d2745002b1040: TOKYO, Nov 20 — Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi got a cold reception in her first outing to China, but Beijing’s “blatant” snub — including a visibly scaled-down welcome — could galvanise her conservative base, experts said on Friday.

Her trip to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit marked the first time she met Chinese President Xi Jinping face-to-face since her comments about Taiwan last year plunged relations between the two major Asian powers to historic lows.

Takaichi suggested that Tokyo could intervene militarily in the event that China attacked Taiwan and a furious China, which views the democratic island as part of its territory, retaliated with trade restrictions and warned its citizens not to travel to Japan.

That backdrop meant “there was little she could expect” from the trip, and “little was indeed achieved in terms of Japan-China relations”, Noriyuki Kawamura, a professor emeritus at Nagoya University of Foreign Studies, told AFP.
Takaichi, as expected, failed to secure a formal sit-down with Xi on the Apec sidelines.

She was greeted by relatively low-ranking officials on arrival in Shenzhen and without the elaborate performances that welcomed other world leaders, prompting headlines at home about China’s “blatant” snub.
Takaichi was also seen struggling to step off her plane because of what appeared to be an unusually large gap between the plane’s door and the top of the boarding stairs.
That prompted online speculation it had been done intentionally by Beijing to embarrass her.
Cold shoulder

A mostly expressionless Xi twice exchanged handshakes with Takaichi during the two-day forum — first very briefly and then for about 10 seconds as he listened to her speak with a beaming smile on her face.
However, experts say the cold shoulder might not be all bad news for her domestically, potentially stoking support from the most hardcore of pro-Takaichi voters.
“The way they see it, she didn’t give in to the snub she got, but shook hands with (Xi) as many as two times with dignity,” Kawamura said.

Yu Uchiyama, a political science professor at the University of Tokyo, also told AFP that China’s chilly reception was unlikely to cost her popularity at home, pointing out that public support for her didn’t wane even after her Taiwan statement a year ago.
“I wouldn’t be surprised to see her loyal supporters become upset by the way she was mocked and grow more resentful toward China,” Uchiyama said.

A day after the summit ended, China again said Japan’s “most urgent task is to correct its wrong words and actions on the Taiwan issue as soon as possible”, according to a foreign ministry spokesman in Beijing.
Takaichi’s critics at home, however, saw the Apec summit as proof of Japan’s diminished global standing under her stewardship and her lack of diplomatic acumen.
Footage circulated widely online of Takaichi approaching President Donald Trump after a group photo and patting him on the back, only to be ignored by the US leader who instead walked away with Xi.
That viral image, coupled with Trump’s historic trilateral summit with Xi and Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, fed social media narratives that she is not taken seriously on the global stage.
“Since when did Japan become such a shameful country? The whole world is laughing at us,” one post on X said.
“It is fatal that Trump — the leader of Japan’s ally — ignores her like this. How much is she hated?” another said.
Still, concerns for Japan’s global reputation could easily be swept aside by a recent surge in distrust towards foreigners that will ultimately help sustain Takaichi’s popularity, Uchiyama said.

Complaints about overtourism and soaring land prices linked to foreign investment have sparked Takaichi’s push for tighter control of visa rules, prompting voters sceptical on immigration to coalesce around her policies.

On the back of this simmering sentiment “resembling xenophobia”, Uchiyama said, it is possible that “people will start to think, ‘why is Takaichi treated so badly overseas when she works so hard in her own country?’” — AFP

619d6175f42ebc85: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 20 — Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) has debuted with a score of 99 out of 100 on review aggregator Metacritic, tying The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the highest rating in the site’s history.
The achievement comes nearly three decades after Nintendo’s 1998 classic established the benchmark, with GTA VI now sitting atop Metacritic’s all-time rankings.

Critics have been almost universally effusive. IGN’s Luke Reilly described the game as “unprecedented, unbelievable, unmissable,” while The Washington Post’s Gene Park called it the most extraordinary game he has ever reviewed.
According to Forbes’ Paul Tassi, 80 of the first 109 reviews awarded the game a perfect score.

The Guardian’s Keza MacDonald praised Rockstar for creating “the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen,” while The New York Times’ Yussef Cole noted that the series has matured beyond its earlier focus on car crashes and stickups.
However, the reception is not without criticism. Several reviewers flagged the game’s 30 frames-per-second performance on consoles and a slow-paced opening.
Metacritic notes that the 99 score could still fluctuate as additional reviews are submitted.
GTA VI launched on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.
a80ebbe7ee9eee87: TAWAU, Nov 20 — A palm oil transporter was sentenced to 30 years’ jail by the High Court after pleading guilty to murdering his female co-worker with a machete over personal dissatisfaction.

Judicial Commissioner Steve Ritikos ordered Roger Pasague Cullano, 54, to serve his sentence from the date of his arrest on June 14, 2025, and to be referred to the Malaysian Immigration Department upon completion of his prison term.
Roger was spared whipping due to his age. He had earlier pleaded guilty to murdering his fellow countrywoman, Abigail Diego Mandi, after the charge was read out by an interpreter in Visayan.
The father of two committed the offence in a bush area at Ample Land Tingkayu Estate, Kunak, between 9.30am and 10.15am on June 13, 2025.

The offence was framed under Section 302 of the Penal Code, which provides for the death penalty or imprisonment of between 30 and 40 years, with not less than 12 strokes of the cane if the death penalty is not imposed.

Based on the facts of the case, the victim was found by her son, Khasmer Diego Rhadzman, lying face down beneath a pile of oil palm fronds and bushes, with her trousers pulled down to her knees and her shirt raised to chest level. She also had several injuries to her head and face.

Earlier, Khasmer had gone to the location at about 10am to collect loose oil palm fruits after receiving a call from his mother. However, he could not find her and instead saw the accused nearby, covered in mud, with bloodstains on his cheek and holding a long machete.
During questioning after his arrest, Roger admitted to killing the victim because he was dissatisfied with her. He also admitted to attacking her with a machete, causing her death.
Deputy Public Prosecutor Mohd Fillany Siji prosecuted, while the accused was represented by lawyers Kamarudin Mohmad Chinki and Prem Elmer Ganasan.
In his submission for an appropriate sentence, Mohd Fillany said the accused had not only taken the life of a mother but had also caused trauma to her son, who discovered her body.

He said, considering the brutal nature of the murder and attack, as well as the absence of mitigating circumstances such as mental incapacity or grave and sudden provocation, the prosecution sought a prison term of between 30 and 35 years, taking into account the accused’s early guilty plea.

Meanwhile, Kamarudin, in his mitigation plea, urged the court to consider the accused’s age, educational background, social circumstances, family responsibilities and potential for rehabilitation when determining the sentence.

He said the guilty plea had saved court time and costs while sparing witnesses and the victim’s family from the emotional strain of giving evidence and undergoing cross-examination during a lengthy trial.

He added that the accused, now 54, was previously married, but his wife died in the Philippines several years ago. They have two children who are currently under the care of the accused’s family members. — Daily Express
8bed89c87235ddda: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 20 — The Malaysian Palm Oil Board (MPOB) is investigating a complaint alleging the blending of imported cooking oil with local supplies, and the relabelling of products for export as Malaysian products.

MPOB confirmed it received an official complaint on the matter, which is now under investigation to establish the validity of the allegations and examine whether any laws, regulations or licensing conditions within MPOB’s jurisdiction have been breached.
“The investigation includes a review of relevant records and documents, including data on the import, processing, storage and export of palm oil by the parties concerned.
“Cross-checks are also being carried out on blending activity records and shipping documents to identify any inconsistencies or discrepancies in the information,” it said in a statement today.

MPOB said the blending of palm oil and palm-based products is part of the industry’s processing activities, subject to compliance with licensing conditions, quality standards and the applicable legal provisions.
However, it said any act of providing false or misleading information about a product’s country of origin is a serious matter that must be addressed.
“The determination of the country of origin of export products must comply with the applicable Rules of Origin, including product-specific criteria under the relevant trade agreements.

“In this regard, the Preferential Certificate of Origin (PCO) is issued by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) to enable exporters to enjoy reduced or exempted tariffs under free trade agreements (FTAs), subject to compliance with the stipulated conditions,” it said.
According to MPOB, the Non-Preferential Certificate of Origin (NPCO) is usually issued by chambers of commerce or trade associations appointed by MITI.
However, for exports to the United States, the issuance of the NPCO has been taken over entirely by MITI with effect from May 6, 2025, it said.
“The determination of origin must be made based on the origin criteria stipulated for the product and export destination concerned,” it said.

Should the investigation find evidence of a breach of the law or licensing conditions within its jurisdiction, appropriate action will be taken under the provisions of the Malaysian Palm Oil Board Act 1998 (Act 582) and related regulations, said MPOB.

A local news portal recently reported that a businessman lodged a complaint on Oct 19 over allegations that Indonesian refined, bleached and deodorised (RBD) palm olein was blended with Malaysian crude palm olein aboard tanker vessel MT Eunice at Port Klang on Sept 30. — Bernama
d201273e0cd0c980: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 20 — The Court of Appeal today described the actions of a man who sodomised and murdered a nine-month-old baby boy, who was under his wife’s care, as an act of extreme cruelty, inhuman and egregious violence against a helpless infant.

Court of Appeal judge Datuk Hayatul Akmal Abdul Aziz said the actions of the respondent, Mohamed Badruldin Mohamed, 41, demonstrated a blatant disregard for responsibility and a profound betrayal of the trust placed in his family.

“The victim was a nine-month-old boy entrusted by his mother to the respondent’s wife for childcare while she was at work. The respondent abused the trust and opportunity afforded to him, subjecting the victim to abuse, including sodomy, before ultimately causing his death by smothering, which obstructed his airways.
“A clear message must be sent to both the respondent and society at large that such crimes are utterly abhorrent, and the only appropriate ultimate penalty is the death sentence.

“Consequently, the prosecution’s appeal is allowed. The sentence of 30 years’ imprisonment and 12 strokes of the cane imposed by the High Court is set aside and replaced with the death sentence by hanging for the murder offence under Section 302 of the Penal Code,” she said when delivering the court’s decision.
The appeal was heard by a panel comprising Judge Datuk Azman Abdullah, who chaired the proceedings, and Judge Datuk Meor Hashimi Abdul Hamid.
In the judgment, Hayatul Akmal said the sentence imposed by the Shah Alam High Court was inadequate.

“We have referred to the post-mortem report, which clearly documented injuries and bruising to the victim’s anus and lips, with the findings consistent with the cause of death, namely smothering. These injuries illustrate the cruelty and extraordinary pain that an innocent infant was forced to endure.

“A chemist also confirmed that the respondent’s sperm DNA was found in anal and rectal swabs taken from the victim. These findings indicate that the infant boy was sodomised by the respondent, the very person entrusted with ensuring his safety,” she said.
She further said the High Court judge had failed to provide reasonable justification for the sentence imposed.

“The High Court judge placed excessive weight on the respondent’s mitigating factors, namely his desire to reintegrate into society and become a better father, thereby sidelining the gravity of the crime committed against an innocent infant.

“In our view, the High Court judge overlooked the heinous nature of the offence, the substantive law and the magnitude of the crime. The failure to recognise its gravity necessitates our intervention to uphold substantive justice and correct a miscarriage of justice,” she said.

The prosecution appealed against the Shah Alam High Court’s decision on Nov 21, 2025, which sentenced Mohamed Badruldin to 30 years’ imprisonment and 12 strokes of the cane after he pleaded guilty to murdering the infant at a residential unit in the Lembah Subang People’s Housing Project (PPR), Ara Damansara, between 8am and 3.30pm on April 27, 2021.
Apart from the murder charge, Mohamed Badruldin was also charged with committing carnal intercourse against the order of nature with the same victim, an offence under Section 377C of the Penal Code.

The offence was committed between 11am and noon on the same day at the same location. The High Court sentenced him to 10 years’ imprisonment and one stroke of the cane, with the prison term to run concurrently with the sentence for murder.
However, the prosecution did not appeal against the sentence for the sodomy offence.

At today’s proceedings, the prosecution was represented by Deputy Public Prosecutor Norshazwani Ishak, while Mohamed Badruldin was represented by lawyers Datuk Mohtarudin Baki and Jayananda Rao. — Bernama
2f8a517a7631fddc: NOVEMBER 20 — Hilaire Barnett’s Constitutional and Administrative Law is a book that has been trusted over generations, equipping its readers with a thorough understanding of the United Kingdom (UK)’s constitutional and administrative law. It is an indispensable guide to this complex area of the law.
On the constitutional concept and convention of collective responsibility, the Senior Lecturer in Law at Queen Mary & Westfield College, University of London explains as follows:

“The convention of collective Cabinet responsibility emphasises the unanimity of government and its accountability to Parliament. The classic expression of collective responsibility remains that of Lord Salisbury:

For all that passes in Cabinet every member of it who does not resign is absolutely and irretrievably responsible and has no right afterwards to say that he agreed in one case to a compromise, while in another he was persuaded by his colleagues… It is only on the principle that absolute responsibility is undertaken by every member of the Cabinet, who, after a decision is arrived at, remains a member of it, that the joint responsibility of Ministers to Parliament can be upheld and one of the essential principles of parliamentary responsibility established.

“The rationale for the convention lies in the need for government to present a united front to Parliament and the public in order to maintain confidence. A government which exhibits public disagreements over policy matters is one which will be regarded as weak, and will be subjected to challenges to its authority to continue in office.

“Two principal sub-rules underlie collective responsibility. The first rule is that, once an agreement is reached in Cabinet, all Members of Cabinet … are bound to speak in support of the decision. There should be no criticism or dissent from the decision in public — irrespective of whether or not the particular member of Cabinet was party to the discussion.
“Equally, if a decision is reached by the Prime Minister in Cabinet Committee or the Inner Cabinet when only a small handful of Members are present, the decision binds all.

“The second supporting rule is that records of Cabinet discussions are absolutely secret. The knowledge that Cabinet records are protected by confidentiality, enhances the opportunity for Members of Cabinet to discuss matters freely, secure in the knowledge that their personal point of view, whatever the decision, will be protected from the public gaze.
“These principles are expressed in ‘Questions of Procedure for Ministers’ in the following manner:

Collective responsibility requires that Ministers should be able to express their views frankly in the expectation that they can argue freely in private while maintaining a united front when decisions have been reached. This in turn requires that the privacy of opinions expressed in Cabinet and Ministerial Committees should be maintained. Moreover, Cabinet and Committee documents will often contain information which needs to be protected in the national interest. It is therefore essential that Ministers take the necessary steps to ensure that they and their staff preserve the privacy of Cabinet business and protect the security of government documents.”
In simple words, collective responsibility means that Ministers must, like the three musketeers, act ‘all for one, and one for all’ failing which they must resign.

The above is also stated by the great scholar, observer, popular teacher and good friend of Malaysia, Professor RH Hickling in An Introduction to the Federal Constitution, where the learned author said:

“It is this principle of collective responsibility that constitutes the most peculiar feature of what we call Cabinet government. All the Ministers are collectively responsible to Parliament, and if one of them refuses to accept the views of his colleagues, then he is expected to resign: for the Ministers stand or fall together.

“This is, in effect, an illustration of the principle of the rule of the majority, or what is sometimes called ‘government by consent’ in which those who disagree with the majority are nevertheless expected to accept their views.

“This, also, is the reason for the secrecy surrounding meetings of the Cabinet, and the brevity of Cabinet minutes, that is, the records of meetings of the Cabinet: for once policy has been decided by the Cabinet, it must be defended in Parliament by all members of the Cabinet.
“Ministers are, therefore, in the position of Dumas’ three musketeers: they must act ‘all for one, and one for all’, and if they fail to conform to this high ideal they must resign.”
* This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
b6568a83ad3eb74a: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 20 — GBS Malaysia is targeting 50 companies for an artificial intelligence (AI) adoption programme that will allow businesses to test AI solutions through complimentary three-month proofs of concept before making longer-term investment decisions.

The PIKOM–GBS Malaysia AI Sandbox Programme covers four areas: customer experience, IT shared services, finance operations and general AI automation. Participating companies will identify business challenges, work with matched solution providers and evaluate results through a shared assessment framework.

Potential applications include customer service responsiveness, IT support, reporting, reconciliation, document processing and repetitive administrative tasks. The evaluation will also consider productivity, service quality, business outcomes and the implications of AI adoption for employees, data and governance.

Six solution providers are participating in the programme: Daythree AI Labs, Grafilab, Revolab.ai, Sabah Net, SHRDC and Talbotiq Technologies. Their expertise covers AI voice agents, operational intelligence, private AI, automation and workforce development.

Datuk Raymond Davadass, Chair of GBS Malaysia, said the initiative reflected the industry’s need to move beyond operational excellence and take on a greater strategic role in addressing business challenges.
“Malaysia must not be content with being where the world’s work gets done. We must aspire to be where the world’s business challenges get solved,” he said.
He said technology adoption should be measured by the business value it creates.
“AI is not our strategy. AI is an enabler of our strategy. The objective isn’t how much AI we deploy. It’s how much business value we create,” he said.

The programme was announced at the GBS Global Summit 2026, which marked the 20th anniversary of GBS Malaysia. Held under the theme “Borderless Intelligence: Connecting Minds. Empowering Business.”, the event brought together about 1,000 delegates from more than 35 countries, over 45 speakers, more than 40 exhibition booths and 75 supporting partners.
Malaysia’s GBS industry recorded 749 entities, representing a 66.8 per cent increase against the baseline, according to the GBS Malaysia Strategy Mid-Term Report 2022–2027, published in 2025.

Industry investments increased 13.5 times, from RM730 million in 2021 to RM9.87 billion in 2024. The sector also recorded 36,626 jobs created since 2021, as at mid-2025, while GBS market revenue was estimated at RM28.14 billion for 2025.
Raymond said the industry had demonstrated its ability to deliver operational excellence over its first 20 years, but its next phase would require greater strategic relevance.

He said collaboration between industry, government, academia and technology providers was important to Malaysia’s competitiveness and its ability to support increasingly sophisticated regional and global business mandates.

Meanwhile, PIKOM chairman Adjunct Practice Prof. Alex Liew outlined three priorities for Malaysia’s GBS industry: strengthening the delivery of higher-value services, helping people progress with the industry through skills development, and making collaboration a competitive strength.

“When an enterprise chooses where to locate its global services, it places confidence in an entire ecosystem: its people, infrastructure, tech providers and institutions. Our responsibility is to ensure that Malaysia continues to earn that confidence,” he said in his opening speech at the Summit.

Selangor Executive Councillor for Investment, Trade and Mobility Ng Sze Han, who officiated the summit, said, “Today, Global Business Services sit at the heart of digital transformation, innovation and economic growth. GBS will keep evolving with AI, automation and digital technology. The Selangor State Government will walk side by side with the private sector. We provide the infrastructure, we build the talent, and we keep Selangor a business-friendly place for your company to grow.”
GBS Malaysia also formalised a strategic Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Cyberview and launched a synthesis report prepared by Cyberview in collaboration with the industry body.

The collaboration featured alongside discussions on digital infrastructure and high-value industries, including a Cyberview side-track titled “Beyond Infrastructure: Powering the Next Wave of High-Value Industries”.

Other discussions covered enterprise transformation, workforce capabilities, cybersecurity, responsible AI and global investment. The agenda also addressed the need for practical reskilling, role redesign and leadership to prepare employees for changing work requirements.
The event concluded with a “Global Outlook 2027: Voices from the Floor” session, bringing together industry perspectives on priorities for the year ahead.
c1cb73c3d8571045: From Kua Kia Soong
The controversy over the RM1,000 land premium for the 99-year lease renewal of the Kuala Lumpur and Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall (KLSCAH) has become another occasion for racial politicking.
Some have portrayed the decision as an unjustified privilege for a Chinese organisation, while others have defended it as a concession to the Chinese community.
Both sides are missing the bigger issue: whether Malaysia genuinely respects its historical and cultural heritage or allows commercial development and political expediency to take precedence.

Established in 1923, KLSCAH is more than a Chinese communal building. It has played an important role in Kuala Lumpur's political, social and cultural history and has been used by Malaysians of different ethnic groups and political affiliations.
Its significance should be assessed in the context of national history, rather than reduced to the racial identity of its users.

The controversy also raises a more fundamental question: why is the preservation of historical buildings and cultural institutions in Malaysia so often treated as an inconvenience rather than a public responsibility?
Monorail and disregard for historical landmarks
Consider the fate of Kuala Lumpur's historic temples.

The Guan Yin temple, established in the 1890s or possibly earlier, is one of the city's historic places of worship. Located beside the Maharajalela Monorail station, its historical setting and architectural character are overshadowed by the surrounding concrete infrastructure.
The temple has survived fires, Kuala Lumpur's transformation and generations of change. Yet how much consideration was given to its historical setting when the monorail infrastructure was introduced?
Modern public transport is undoubtedly necessary. But must modernisation mean historical buildings are reduced to insignificant structures dwarfed by concrete and steel?
This is not an argument against public transport, but for intelligent urban planning that allows modern infrastructure and historical landmarks to coexist.
The Sydney Monorail, for instance, was decommissioned in 2013 and dismantled in 2014 as part of the city's transition to light rail.
Another new development now threatens the Guan Yin temple. The authorities should assess its impact on the historic precinct before any damage becomes irreversible.
The wider Chinese community should also be asking why more has not been done to protect such landmarks.
Kuala Lumpur is destroying its own history
The fate of other historical buildings in Kuala Lumpur should prompt reflection on our priorities.
Pudu Jail, built in 1895, was once among the city's most recognisable landmarks. Its imposing walls and famous mural formed part of Kuala Lumpur's physical and social history.
The prison complex was demolished in stages, with most of the buildings gone by 2012. Only sections of its exterior wall and entrance were retained.

Whatever one's views on the colonial prison system, Pudu Jail was part of our history. Its preservation could have provided an important historical and educational site. Instead, most of it disappeared.
Then there was Bok House, a neo-classical mansion built in 1929 by businessman Chua Cheng Bok along Jalan Ampang. It also housed the well-known restaurant Le Coq d'Or.

Despite appeals by heritage advocates, the mansion was demolished in 2006. The argument that it lacked sufficient historical value illustrated how little importance was attached to architectural heritage.
The Cathay cinema, another familiar Kuala Lumpur landmark, also disappeared in the name of urban redevelopment.
How many more buildings must we lose before we realise that a city is not defined merely by its shopping malls, luxury condominiums and skyscrapers?
The Sultan Abdul Samad Building, Central Market and historic buildings around Dataran Merdeka have fortunately survived.
But their survival should not be an excuse for complacency. They require continued conservation, proper maintenance and protection from insensitive development.
Malaysia's collective memory under threat
This is not simply a Chinese community issue.

Malaysia's heritage includes Malay villages, traditional wooden houses, mosques, Indian temples, colonial buildings, indigenous settlements, archaeological sites, historic cemeteries and natural landscapes.

The demolition of the Sri Uchimalai Muniswarar Temple in Rawang in February was another painful reminder of the vulnerability of places of worship with longstanding community ties. The temple was demolished after the landowner sought possession of the site.

The controversy over the 130-year-old Dewi Sri Pathrakaliamman Temple on Jalan Masjid India, Kuala Lumpur, also raised fundamental questions about how development should accommodate historic places of worship.

Although the authorities subsequently identified a replacement site, the episode showed how vulnerable such institutions can be when land ownership and development interests take precedence over historical continuity.

We should also remember the traditional Malay kampungs lost to urban redevelopment, indigenous communities displaced by development projects and historic landscapes sacrificed to commercial interests.
The heritage of the Orang Asli and indigenous peoples of Sabah and Sarawak deserves the same protection as Kuala Lumpur's old temples and shophouses.
A nation that remembers only the history of its politically powerful communities has a distorted understanding of itself.

Developers should be required to assess the historical, cultural and social significance of buildings and places of worship before obtaining development approvals. Where possible, they should preserve these sites in their original locations rather than treating relocation as the default solution.

In the latest KLSCAH controversy, critics who believe public institutions should not receive special consideration for heritage preservation must explain why the same principle should not apply to every other historic building, temple, mosque, church, traditional settlement and cultural institution in Malaysia.

Should a historic Malay institution be required to pay commercial land premiums even when its land is designated for institutional use? Should an Indian temple be denied consideration simply because its preservation benefits a particular religious community?
We must reject this absurd racial arithmetic.
The question is not whether KLSCAH is Chinese, Malay or Indian. It is whether the institution has historical, cultural and public significance that deserves protection.
Kua Kia Soong is a former MP and a former director of Suaram.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

1f9a8e02603730e4: Welcome to Friday and therefore to another edition of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed tech support column in which we share your tales of cleaning up messes made by clients and colleagues.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Dennis" who told us he once ran a tech support business in a major US city.
"I got a call from a very well-known lawyer's office," he told On Call. "Over the two decades I spent supporting his office, this attorney and I became close friends."
The attorney was also a good client because Dennis found himself billing a three-figure sum every month for malware removal that resulted from the lawyer’s – ahem – personal browsing habits.
Dennis eventually tired of malware removal and told his client to expect a substantial bill for the iMac he was about to buy as a replacement for his PC.
"I told him this would pay for itself in 18 months," Dennis wrote, because he figured it wouldn't get malware all the time.
"He actually said, with genuine concern: 'If you do that, you will make less money'."
Dennis replied that he aimed to give his clients the best advice, and that on this occasion his counsel was to pay Apple instead of himself!
"It took him about five years to stumble across anything that could harm that iMac," Dennis wrote. "When he did, I had no idea what to do: I had never seen an infected Apple product."
So he did what all tech support people do: reinstalled the OS and crossed his fingers.
Dennis was rewarded when the machine came back to life, with all data and settings intact.

"I had given up at least $6,000 in support revenue by solving his problem and I'd do it again," he wrote, before winding up his story by letting us know "I retired five years ago. It’s still on his desk!"

b7f674ad7efc71b2: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant behind Claude, has just pulled off the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history. The company raised US$81 billion by listing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market, beating the previous all-time record of US$75 billion set by SpaceX earlier this year. Initially set at $US83, Anthropic’s share price soared to US$111 after its debut, briefly nudging the company’s value past US$2 trillion, before falling again as investors took profits. The blockbuster stock market listing comes at a nervous moment in the AI sector. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the huge sums of money being poured into the AI boom are justified, and many are reducing their exposure to technology stocks. Adding to this shakiness has been the shock departure of chipmaker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, following an affair scandal. Anthropic’s debut certainly sets a benchmark for rival OpenAI, which still plans to go public. But we shouldn’t mistake investor enthusiasm in one company for a broader vote of confidence in the global AI industry. What does Anthropic’s performance tell us? One thing we can learn from this week’s result is that there is a huge amount of demand for Anthropic itself. Strong revenue was one factor. At the end of October, Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate (an estimate of yearly revenue based on the previous month) was US$81 billion. But the company’s popularity likely also played a role. Claude is one of the most widely used AI tools around the globe. “Familiarity bias” is a well known phenomenon in investing. Intense demand meant many smaller investors missed out on getting shares ahead of the official listing. Last week, Bloomberg reported the share offering was about six times oversubscribed. According to the Wall Street Journal, only about 15% of available shares were ultimately allocated to retail investors. Is Anthropic’s huge valuation justified? Anthropic’s share price closed the day at US$97.17, up 17% from its IPO price, which values the company at US$1.76 trillion. That’s slightly less than where SpaceX landed at the end of its first day, at US$2.1 trillion. But it’s still a colossal figure, even accounting for the fact that Anthropic beat OpenAI to generating a quarterly operating profit earlier this year (before returning to an operating loss the following quarter). For Anthropic, like any company, going public should make it easier to raise large amounts of capital. That could be important for a company which has already made about US$900 billion in future spending commitments – mostly on computing infrastructure – between now and 2045. However, it’s important to look at how these commitments play out in the short and long term. About half of this spending is due by 2030. The near-term bill over the next 12 months is about US$70 billion, which is manageable with its current revenue run rate of US$81 billion. Other concerns may be more pressing. Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 47% – which is strong – but this compares to a growth rate of 144% in the second quarter. This suggests a sharp slowdown in growth overall. Token prices have also been falling, driven in part by more competition from cheaper AI models. Also on revenue, the company has warned that some of its customers – “particularly early-stage and high-growth companies” – rely on external financing. This could reduce their spending with Anthropic if that financing dries up. What to watch after this public listing For any company, listing on a public stock exchange introduces much more scrutiny. Previously, the focus on Anthropic has centred on its technology and growth potential. Now, there’ll be a renewed focus on corporate governance. Beyond the financial metrics of revenue growth, profitability, cash flow and more, investors will now more closely scrutinise how management balances commercial returns with AI safety, privacy and social responsibility. Speaking just before the Nasdaq listing, Chief Executive Dario Amodei acknowledged people’s serious safety concerns: We have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. But he expressed faith in Anthropic’s ability to get the balance right: If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. Protesters staged major rallies outside the Nasdaq exchange’s New York headquarters and outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters. They called for stronger government regulation and a slowdown or total pause on AI development. What does this mean for rival OpenAI? Another of the world’s major AI companies, OpenAI, had initially planned its own public listing this year. However, it has now ruled this out until 2027, citing safety concerns around the technology. Anthropic’s IPO creates both opportunities and challenges for its rival. On the plus side, Anthropic’s performance gives OpenAI and potential investors a yardstick – including financial performance benchmarks and lots of other useful information. But now that Anthropic has become a publicly listed company, this industry is about to come under even more intense scrutiny. If public sentiment about AI worsens between now and when OpenAI launches its IPO, it could pay a steep price. 81c3e216ae69d9cd: Big Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which says the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice.

BEUC said: "Big Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products."

The European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023, imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition.

The devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on.

BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026.

In the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the company used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from users for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine.

"Microsoft also regularly prompts users who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC said.

Then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store users to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications.

The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge users into handing over their data.

Apple announced new terms for developers earlier this year in response to its App Store dispute with the European Commission, but BEUC said it was "concerned that the new terms do not resolve fundamental non-compliance issues."

Google did not respond to requests for comment from The Register. A Microsoft spokesperson told us: "We are continuing to engage with the Commission and industry at large to ensure Microsoft's designated platforms comply fully with the DMA."

An Amazon spokesperson told The Register “Our consent experience is clear and gives customers informed choice about how their personal information is used across Amazon services. We see that in practice.

“A seller that uses Amazon Stores in the EU can offer the same products on any third-party online marketplace or its own direct to customer website at any price, without affecting their eligibility to be highlighted as the Featured Offer. This is set out clearly in our DMA Compliance Report.”

BEUC director general Agustín Reyna said: "The era of cosmetic compliance must end. It is high time the Commission holds gatekeepers to account and imposes dissuasive penalties in all cases where they bypass the DMA's rules."
The report has been shared with the Commission. Whether BEUC's allegations lead to further findings of non-compliance or penalties is now a matter for the regulator. ®

f6c9acbf276d0e53: The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.

That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast (R-FL), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.
The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items.
BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance.
But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent.

Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies, the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security.
Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft.
Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons.
A diverting drama

The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The New York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation.

Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law.
One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.”

Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk.
Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions.
Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact.
Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday said that new ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow.

Alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the company’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the new policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.”
“Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure plan,” he said.
But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028.
Alibaba’s Wu predicted his company “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed.
Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors.
And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments.
That’s likely because Beijing needs to approve imports and chose not to do so while its own chipmakers develop improved products. ®

70925270e972fdaf: TOKYO, Nov 20 — Inflation in Japan picked up again in October due to rising food prices and energy costs, official data showed Friday, boosting the likelihood of an interest rate hike.
Excluding volatile fresh produce, inflation was 2.2 per cent, up from 2.1 per cent in September, according to the Internal Affairs Ministry reading.
The latest figure is slightly below the 2.3 per cent expected by experts surveyed by Bloomberg.

Soaring energy costs due to the Middle East conflict as well as a weak yen are pushing up prices of imported products, including food. Energy prices also rose sharply as the government scaled back subsidies for gasoline and electricity that had helped mitigate the impact of the war.
The cost of electricity rose 1.6 per cent in October from a year ago, compared to a drop of 2.4 per cent in September, while the price of gas jumped 5.3 per cent compared with a 0.2 per cent rise.
Marcel Thieliant of Capital Economics said the subsidy scale back had played a role as “electricity inflation turned positive for the first time in a year”.
“While the government will reinstate subsidies over the winter, those subsidies aren’t any more generous than usual,” he said.
“With unsubsidised tariffs reaching a record high, utilities prices will soon rise at a double-digit pace.”
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has pledged another round of subsidies to meet rising energy demand in winter, while also pushing a two-year consumption tax cut scheme for food from next year.
Still, analysts have noted the persistent weakness of the yen as a key factor boosting consumer prices.

The Bank of Japan declared last month that inflation had hit its two per cent target, and is expected to trend “clearly above 2 percent” in months to come, driven by rising prices of a wide range of products and services, including those related to artificial intelligence demand, such as semiconductors.
The inflation figure Friday is likely to strengthen the central bank’s case for further tightening of monetary policy.
Japanese officials are expected to hike interest rates in December as inflationary pressure builds. — AFP
